I need to calculate inter-rater agreement (2 annotators) on a small dataset (let's say 10 items), where annotators used between 1 and 4 labels per item. Based on everything I've read, Krippendorff's alpha seems to be the thing I should use, but I can't figure out how to use it with multi-label data instead of single-label data. How can I measure inter-rater agreement with multi-label data? ## 1 Answer 1. First one is how to calculate agreement in case of multi-label annotation. The second one is what function to use, in R or in a different language, to do this calculation. The answer to first question is that you should:. Here is explained how to calculate Krippendorff's alpha for multi-label annotation using MASI distance using Python. from nltk.metrics import masi_distance. task_data = [('coder1','Item0',frozenset(['l1','l2'])),. I have not found any implementation Krippendorff's alpha in R that lets you use custom distance function as nltk.metrics.agreement does. The solution is to use irrCAC library, as it's krippen.alpha function accepts the weight matrix as argument. Than, one can calculate the weight matrix for all observed combination of labels using any distance function. I call python to calculate MASI distance. dataset <- data.frame(matrix(dataset,ncol = 2, byrow = T), stringsAsFactors = F). #function that calculates MASI distance using python nltk.metrics. masi <- function(x,y,split = " "). if(length(str_split(x,split,simplify = F)) == 1). x <- str_split(x,split,simplify = F). x <- unlist(str_split(x,split,simplify = F)). if(length(str_split(y,split,simplify = F)) == 1). y <- str_split(y,split,simplify = F). y <- unlist(str_split(y,split,simplify = F)). masiD <- nltk$masi_distance(pybuiltins$set(x),pybuiltins$set(y)). #calculating weight matrix for all observed combination of lables using MASI distance. krippen.alpha.raw(dataset, weights = distMasi,categ.labels = rownames(distMasi)). ## Your Answer. results.title: Krippendorff’s Alpha for Annotation Agreement | Label Studio
results.content: # How to Use Krippendorff’s Alpha to Measure Annotation Agreement. As a part of our inter-annotator agreement series, we’re digging into one of the most flexible and widely applicable metrics out there: Krippendorff’s alpha. Compared to other agreement metrics like Cohen’s kappa or Fleiss’ kappa, Krippendorff’s alpha offers more flexibility—and is better suited for real-world data annotation workflows. This makes it particularly useful for messy, real-world datasets where not all annotators rate every item or where the labels span beyond simple yes/no categories. Krippendorff’s alpha requires you to define an agreement metric between rating categories. Observed agreement is the average agreement across all rated items, normalized by the number of raters and label options. We’ll replace rik with the value in the table for each item i and rating k, and sum these results. Even if you don’t compute it manually, understanding how Krippendorff’s alpha works helps you choose the right agreement metric—and take action when results are low.

Krippendorff’s alpha () is a reliability coefficient developed to measure the agreement among observers, coders, judges, raters, annotators or measuring instruments drawing distinctions among…. ### On The Krippendorff's Alpha Coefficient. This paper proposes a simple procedure for calculating the Krippendorff’s alpha that involves simple calculations similar to those needed to obtain the Pi coefficient of Fleiss (1971), and presents some alternative agreement coefficients, which address the classical problem of the paradoxes associated with Cohen's Kappa. ### Agreement and Information in the Reliability of Coding. The concept of reliability, simple agreement, three conceptions of chance to correct that agreement, and sources of information deficiency are explored, and two measures of information about reliability, akin to the power of a statistical test, are developed. ### krippendorffsalpha: An R Package for Measuring Agreement Using Krippendorff's Alpha Coefficient.
